pr.body:
### Issue Link :link:
Fixes #3184

### Goals :soccer:
This PR fixes the encoding of `Decimal` values using `URLEncodedFormEncoder`.

### Implementation Details :construction:
`Decimal`'s native `Encodable` implementation encodes the full description of the value as an object with all the decimal values broken out. `JSONEncoder` cheats by using `JSONSerialization`'s existing special handling to get around this fact. Instead, we just use `String(describing:)` to build the output `String`, rather than letting the value encode itself. This *should* produce a stable value, but better approaches are appreciated.

issue.title: CRLF injection into multipart bodies via a quoted MediaType parameter

pr.title: Reject CR and LF in quoted MediaType parameters
pr.body:
Fixes #9725

`MediaType` accepts CR and LF inside quoted parameter values. It keeps the original string, and `MultipartBody.writeOrCountBytes` writes that string directly into a part's `Content-Type` header. An untrusted media type can therefore introduce line breaks into the multipart headers.

I excluded CR and LF from the `QUOTED` character class. `toMediaType()` now rejects those values with `IllegalArgumentException`, and `toMediaTypeOrNull()` returns `null`. Parameter whitespace handling is unchanged.

Tests cover CR, LF and CRLF inside a quoted parameter. They run through the existing `MediaTypeTest` subclasses, covering both parsing APIs. The CR case failed before the change because parsing succeeded.

The MediaType tests, the full `:okhttp:jvmTest` suite, `:okhttp:spotlessCheck`, and `./gradlew clean check` pass.

issue.title: AWS Lambda streamHandle ignores writable backpressure and resolves before the response finishes

pr.title: fix(aws-lambda): respect backpressure when streaming the response body
pr.body:
Fixes #5333.

## Problem

`streamToNodeStream` in the AWS Lambda adapter ignored the return value of `writer.write()`:

```ts
while (!readResult.done) {
  writer.write(readResult.value)
  readResult = await reader.read()
}
writer.end()
```

Two consequences:

1. **No backpressure.** Once the response exceeds the destination's `highWaterMark`, `write()` returns `false`, but the loop keeps reading and writing. The whole body accumulates in the writable's internal buffer.
2. **Resolves too early.** `writer.end()` only signals that no more data is coming — it does not mean the stream has finished. `streamHandle` could resolve while `responseStream.writableFinished` was still `false`, so a Lambda invocation could complete before the response had actually been delivered.

## Fix

Read the body through an async generator and hand it to `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`. `pipeline` paces reads against the destination, waits for `finish`, and propagates errors from either side — which is the behaviour the issue asks for, without hand-rolling the stream lifecycle.

`node:` imports are already used elsewhere in the Lambda adapters (`src/adapter/lambda-edge/handler.ts` imports `node:crypto`), and `stream/promises` is available on every Node version that supports Lambda response streaming.

## Tests

`runtime-tests/lambda/stream-backpressure.test.ts` streams 2 MiB in 16 KiB chunks into a slow writable with a 16 KiB `highWaterMark` and asserts that:

- every byte is written by the time the handler resolves,
- `writableFinished` is `true`,
- the source never runs more than a bounded number of chunks ahead of the sink.

Against `main` the first assertion fails with `expected +0 to be 2097152` — the handler resolves before a single chunk has been flushed.

A second test covers a body that errors mid-stream, confirming the handler still logs and resolves rather than rejecting, so the error contract is unchanged.

Full suite passes: 148 files, 5026 tests.

issue.title: LineDecoder is accidentally quadratic: iter_lines() seems to hang forever
issue.body:
When calling `Response.iter_lines()`, things can seem to hang forever.

The problem is that `LineDecoder` is quadratic in it's string copying behaviour. If a 31MB chunk with 18,768 lines is passed in to `LineDecoder()` then it takes 1m45s to process it vs 0.1s for a simple `text.splitlines()`. This is readily reproduced by simply using `LineDecoder()` to decode a file, like `/usr/share/dict/words` (do not attempt, you may be waiting until the heat death of the universe).

It may be a bug somewhere else that `iter_text()` is returning chunks that are too big.

But either way, you probably want to reconsider the wisdom of slicing the string to chop the beginning off it vs. just keeping an index.

You can slice the string before returning from the decoder so it's only done once per chunk.

Anyhoo, thanks for the great work!

issue.title: copy.copy() of a defer_build model's __pydantic_validator__ raises RecursionError
issue.body:
### Initial Checks

- [x] I confirm that I'm using Pydantic V2

### Description

Copying or unpickling the `MockValSer` placeholder that a `defer_build=True` model holds raises `RecursionError`. The new instance has no slots set yet, and `copy`/`pickle` look up `__setstate__` on it. That lookup falls through to `MockValSer.__getattr__`, which reads `self._attempt_rebuild`; reading the unset slot calls `__getattr__` again, until the recursion limit.

We hit it in Ray Serve when cloudpickle ships a model class by value (ray-project/ray#52211). Raising `AttributeError` for the slot names (or underscore names) in `__getattr__` before reading `self._attempt_rebuild` would fix copy and unpickle.

### Example Code

```Python
import copy

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class Model(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)

    x: int


copy.copy(Model.__pydantic_validator__)
```

pr.title: fix(tree): panic in findCaseInsensitivePathRec with RedirectFixedPath
pr.body:
### What

Fixes a panic (`invalid node type`) in `findCaseInsensitivePathRec` that occurs when `RedirectFixedPath` is enabled and a request path doesn't match any registered route.

Fixes #2959

### Root cause

In `findCaseInsensitivePathRec`, when the current node has `wildChild = true`, the code grabs `n.children[0]` to find the wildcard child. But `addChild()` always appends the wildcard child at the **end** of the children array, not the beginning. So when a node has both static children and a wildcard child, `children[0]` points to a static node, and the `switch n.nType` falls through to the `default` case which panics.

The `getValue()` function already handles this correctly on line 483:
```go
// Handle wildcard child, which is always at the end of the array
n = n.children[len(n.children)-1]
```

This PR applies the same fix to `findCaseInsensitivePathRec`.

### Reproduction

```go
router := gin.Default()
router.RedirectFixedPath = true
router.GET("/aa/aa", handler)
router.GET("/:bb/aa", handler)
// GET /aa -> panic: invalid node type
```

### Testing

Added two test cases covering the exact scenarios from the issue:
- Mixed static + param routes under the same prefix
- Verified no panics for unmatched paths
- Verified correct behavior for exact, case-insensitive, and param matches

issue.title: `issue view --comments --json` silently ignores `--comments`
issue.body:
### Describe the bug

Combining `gh issue view --comments` with `--json` silently ignores the `--comments` flag unless `comments` is also explicitly included in the JSON field list.

`--comments` is documented as “View issue comments,” so accepting the combination without an error or warning makes it appear that comments were fetched and included when they were not.

### Steps to reproduce

Using `gh` 2.96.0:

```bash
gh issue view 14209 --repo cli/cli --comments \
  --json number,title,body
```

The resulting JSON contains only `number`, `title`, and `body`; it does not contain `comments`.

### Expected behavior

Either:

1. `--comments` should add `comments` to the requested JSON fields, or
2. `--comments` and `--json` should be mutually exclusive and the command should return a clear validation error.

Silently treating `--comments` as a no-op is surprising and can cause scripts or agents to proceed without issue comments.

### Workaround

Explicitly include `comments`:

```bash
gh issue view 14209 --repo cli/cli \
  --json number,title,body,comments
```

### Additional context

`--comments` is a human-readable output mode rather than shorthand for the JSON `comments` field. In the current implementation, the JSON exporter determines the lookup fields and takes precedence, leaving the parsed comments flag unused.

issue.title: CORS: the middleware misclassifies all OPTIONS requests as preflight requests
issue.body:
### Issue Description

Echo's CORS middleware misclassifies all `OPTIONS` requests as preflight requests, thereby unduly preventing requests from hitting user-registered `OPTIONS` endpoints.

I've previously discussed the general problem on [my personal blog](https://jub0bs.com/posts/2023-02-08-fearless-cors/#4-categorise-requests-correctly) and how Echo suffers from it in issue #2510.

### Checklist

- [x] Dependencies installed
- [x] No typos
- [x] Searched existing issues and docs

### Expected behaviour

(For this section and the next, please refer to the server code below.)

Consider the `OPTIONS` requests resulting from the following two `curl` commands:

```shell
curl -v -XOPTIONS \
  localhost:8080/hello
```
```shell
curl -v -XOPTIONS \
  -H "Origin: https://example.com" \
  localhost:8080/hello
```

According to [the Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-preflight-request), neither request is a preflight request, because
- the first one lacks both an `Origin` header and an `Access-Control-Request-Method` header, and
- the second one lacks an `Access-Control-Request-Method` header.

Therefore, those requests should get through the CORS middleware, exercise the handler registered on `/hello`, and get a response of this kind:

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Allow: GET, OPTIONS
Date: Mon, 23 Oct 2023 12:30:33 GMT
```

In contrast, an `OPTIONS` requests resulting from the following `curl` command is a bona fide preflight request; as such, it should be (and is) intercepted and handled by the CORS middleware:

```shell
curl -v -XOPTIONS \
  -H "Origin: https://example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT" \
  localhost:8080/hello
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Vary: Origin
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Method
Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers
-snip-
```

### Actual behaviour

The first two aforementioned `OPTIONS` requests get intercepted and handled by the CORS middleware rather than by the handler registered on `OPTIONS /hello`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the program to start the server.
2. Exercise it via `curl`(see commands above).

### Working code to debug

```go
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"net/http"

	"github.com/labstack/echo/v4"
	"github.com/labstack/echo/v4/middleware"
)

func main() {
	e := echo.New()
	e.Use(middleware.CORSWithConfig(middleware.CORSConfig{
		AllowOrigins: []string{"*"},
		AllowMethods: []string{http.MethodPut},
	}))
	e.GET("/hello", func(c echo.Context) error {
		return c.String(http.StatusOK, "Hello, World!")
	})
	e.OPTIONS("/hello", func(c echo.Context) error {
		c.Response().Header().Set("Allow", "GET, OPTIONS")
		c.Response().WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
		return nil
	})
	if err := e.Start(":8080"); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
		e.Logger.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

### Version/commit

Echo v4.11.2. See my `go.mod` below:

```
module whatever

go 1.21.3

require github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.11.2

require (
	github.com/golang-jwt/jwt v3.2.2+incompatible // indirect
	github.com/labstack/gommon v0.4.0 // indirect
	github.com/mattn/go-colorable v0.1.13 // indirect
	github.com/mattn/go-isatty v0.0.19 // indirect
	github.com/valyala/bytebufferpool v1.0.0 // indirect
	github.com/valyala/fasttemplate v1.2.2 // indirect
	golang.org/x/crypto v0.14.0 // indirect
	golang.org/x/net v0.17.0 // indirect
	golang.org/x/sys v0.13.0 // indirect
	golang.org/x/text v0.13.0 // indirect

```

pr.title: fix(middleware): classify CORS preflight per Fetch standard
pr.body:
## Problem

CORS middleware treated **every** `OPTIONS` request as a preflight and short-circuited with `204`, so user-registered `OPTIONS` handlers never ran.

Per the [Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-preflight-request), a preflight is an `OPTIONS` request that includes **both**:

- `Origin`
- `Access-Control-Request-Method`

These are **not** preflights and should reach the next handler:

```bash
curl -X OPTIONS localhost:8080/hello
curl -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: https://example.com' localhost:8080/hello
```

This one **is** a preflight and should still be handled by the middleware:

```bash
curl -X OPTIONS \
  -H 'Origin: https://example.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT' \
  localhost:8080/hello
```

Fixes #2534.

## Change

- Add `isCORSPreflight` requiring method + Origin + ACR-Method
- Non-preflight `OPTIONS` continues the chain via `next(c)`
- Real preflights keep the existing short-circuit + CORS headers
- Still copy router `Allow` onto `OPTIONS` responses when present

## Tests

- `TestIsCORSPreflight`
- `TestCORS_NonPreflightOPTIONSPassThrough` (covers the three cases above)
- Existing preflight cases updated to send `Access-Control-Request-Method`

```text
go test ./middleware/ -run 'CORS|IsCORSPreflight'
```

issue.title: Undefined Route Request Leads to Infinite Loop in route matching

pr.title: fix: panic on Mount() when a router is mounted onto itself
pr.body:
## Problem

Mounting a router (or an inline mux derived from it via `With()`/`Group()`, which
shares the same underlying route tree) onto itself causes an infinite loop on any
request that doesn't match a defined route, instead of falling through to a 404:

```go
r := chi.NewRouter().With(middleware.Logger)
r.Mount("/", r.Group(func(r chi.Router) {
    r.Get("/ping", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        w.Write([]byte("pong"))
    })
}))
```

`GET /ping` responds fine, but any undefined path hangs forever. Confirmed this is a
genuine busy-spin, not a deadlock: the process's CPU time climbed ~45s over ~3
wall-clock seconds while a single bad request was in flight, and a goroutine dump on
timeout shows the request cycling forever through
`Mux.ServeHTTP → mountHandler → Mux.ServeHTTP → routeHTTP → ...` with no state change.

Fixes #843.

## Root cause

`With()` and `Group()` return a new inline `*Mux` that shares the *same* underlying
`tree` pointer as the original router rather than copying it. So
`r.Mount("/", r.Group(fn))` wires a mount whose target handler routes through the
exact same tree the mount itself lives in.

In `Mux.ServeHTTP`, once a routing context already exists on the request (i.e. we're
inside a mount), it calls `mx.handler.ServeHTTP(w, r)` directly. `nextRoutePath()`
recomputes `RoutePath` as `"/" + <wildcard capture>` — for a mount at `"/"`, the
capture is the entire remaining path, so `RoutePath` ends up identical to what it was
before. Combined with the shared tree, a request that doesn't match `/ping` falls
through to the same `"/*"` mount node, calls the same `mountHandler`, recomputes the
same `RoutePath`, and re-enters routing with zero state change — an infinite loop
that pins one goroutine per bad request forever (a resource-exhaustion concern for a
router commonly used on public-facing services).

## Fix

`Mount()` now panics immediately — at registration time, not request time — when the
handler being mounted is a `*Mux` that shares the mounting router's tree:

```
chi: attempting to Mount() a router onto itself on '<pattern>'
```

This follows the same runtime-safety philosophy chi already uses elsewhere in
`Mount()` (e.g. panicking on a nil handler or on mounting over an existing pattern),
and mirrors the precedent set in #1148, which fixed a related `Mount()` edge case
with a similar "catch misuse loudly at registration time" approach plus a regression
test in the same style.

The check generalizes beyond the literal repro: it keys off tree-pointer identity, so
it also catches a plain `r.Mount("/", r)` self-mount, and any depth of `With()`/
`Group()` chaining, not just the specific pattern reported in the issue.

## Testing

- Added `TestMountingSelf` in `mux_test.go`, covering both the literal self-mount and
  the `With()`/`Group()` variant from the issue. Verified it fails (no panic) against
  the unpatched code and passes after the f

### Bug Description

`parseSrcset` uses truthiness checks to detect whether a descriptor is already present. The WHATWG parser accepts a density value of zero (`0x`), but the implementation stores it as numeric `0`. As a result, a following descriptor is not recognized as conflicting and is accepted too.

### Link to Minimal Reproduction and steps to reproduce

Repository: https://github.com/webpack/webpack

   ```
3. It returns `[["a.png", 0, 5]]`. Also try `a.png 0x 1w` and `a.png 0x 1h`.


### Expected Behavior

Accept a single `0x` descriptor, but reject a second `x`, `w`, or `h` descriptor in the same candidate with `Invalid srcset descriptor`. In the HTML parser, the invalid value should be reported as a bad `srcset` attribute.

### Actual Behavior

The parser accepts `0x 1x` (and `0x 1w` / `0x 1h`) and returns the URL candidate instead of reporting invalid descriptors.

None

_No response_

The WHATWG “parse a srcset attribute” algorithm accepts zero density (it only rejects density values less than zero) and treats the descriptor as present: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#parse-a-srcset-attribute

pr.title: Default Nested Partial Fix
pr.body:
Fixes #2149

https://github.com/marshmallow-code/marshmallow/commit/59a432971b6cfac86162e06fec30c8f2c4e66b7b regressed the behavior of schemas using `partial` when they are passed to `Nested`. 

The default value for `partial` in schema arguments was normalized to `None` in the few places it was `False`. This ensures that `partial=False` is treated as an explicit request to disable partial loading in nested schemas, and `partial=None` is treated as a request to defer to nested schemas' partial behavior.

This changes the behavior of schemas without `partial` defined when they contain nested schemas with `partial` defined, but the behavior introduced by 3.0.0b19 was untested, undocumented, and counterintuitive, so I am hesitant to label this backwards incompatible.

issue.title: isShallow() returns false for shallow collection proxies (shallowReactive(new Map()))
issue.body:
### Vue version

3.5.43

### Link to minimal reproduction

```js
import { shallowReactive, shallowReadonly, reactive, readonly, isShallow, isReadonly } from 'vue'

// plain objects work
console.log(isShallow(shallowReactive({})))      // true
console.log(isShallow(shallowReadonly({})))      // true

// collections don't
console.log(isShallow(shallowReactive(new Map())))      // false (expected true)
console.log(isShallow(shallowReadonly(new Map())))      // false (expected true)
console.log(isShallow(shallowReactive(new Set())))      // false (expected true)
console.log(isShallow(shallowReadonly(new Set())))      // false (expected true)

// sanity: the deep counterparts correctly report false
console.log(isShallow(reactive(new Map())))      // false
console.log(isReadonly(readonly(new Map())))     // true, so collection traps do handle their own flags
```

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

Call `isShallow()` on a proxy returned by `shallowReactive()` / `shallowReadonly()` where the underlying value is a `Map` or a `Set`.

### What is expected?

`isShallow()` should return `true`, matching the documented contract ("Checks if a value is a shallow reactive or shallow readonly object") and matching the behavior of the plain-object counterparts. `reactive()` / `readonly()` on collections report their flags correctly (e.g. `isReadonly(readonly(new Map()))` is `true`), so `isShallow()` should behave consistently.

### What is actually happening?

`isShallow()` returns `false`, because the collection `get` trap in `packages/reactivity/src/collectionHandlers.ts` (`createInstrumentationGetter`) handles the `__v_isReactive`, `__v_isReadonly` and `__v_raw` flags but not `__v_isShallow`, so the lookup falls through to `Reflect.get(rawTarget, '__v_isShallow')`, which is always `undefined`.

This is not just the predicate itself — `isShallow()` gates several internal code paths, and each of them misbehaves for shallow collections:

- `ref.value = shallowReactive(new Map())` (RefImpl setter) stores `toRaw(value)` and wraps it with `toReactive()`, so the user's shallow proxy is silently replaced by a deep reactive proxy.
- Assigning a shallow collection into a reactive object property (`state.m = shallowReactive(new Map())`) or into another reactive collection (`outerMap.set('m', shallowMap)`) likewise loses the shallow wrapper.
- `watch()` treats a shallow reactive collection as deep (`reactiveGetter` traverses more than one level).
- The devtools custom formatter labels `shallowReactive(new Map())` as `Reactive` instead of `ShallowReactive`.

Note that the existing test `The results of the shallow and readonly assignments are the same (Map)` only covers shallow *plain objects* stored inside a reactive Map, which works today — the collection-proxy case is uncovered.

pr.body:

issue.title: watch: getter source re-evaluation runs `onCleanup` / `onWatcherCleanup` even when the value is unchanged and `cb` is not called (3.6 regression)
issue.body:
### Vue version

3.6.0-rc.10 (also 3.6.0-alpha.1 through rc.10, and `minor` at 44e5092c8; 3.5.43 is fine)

### Link to minimal reproduction

[SFC Playground, Vue 3.6.0-rc.10](https://play.vuejs.org/#) (the same code on 3.5.43 for comparison: [link](https://play.vuejs.org/#))

### Steps to reproduce

Open the playground (Vue 3.6.0-rc.10 is preselected). The watcher logs `cb(true)` on creation.

1. Click **a++**. `a` goes 1 → 2; the getter `() => a.value > 0` still returns `true`, so `cb` is not called.
2. Click **scope.stop()**.

Log on 3.6.0-rc.10:

```
cb(true)
a = 2 (getter still true, cb not called)
  onCleanup
  onWatcherCleanup
scope.stop()
```

Log on 3.5.43 (same code, version switched):

```
cb(true)
a = 2 (getter still true, cb not called)
scope.stop()
  onCleanup
  onWatcherCleanup
```

The same in plain Node (`npm i vue@3.6.0-rc.10`):

```js
const { ref, watch, effectScope, nextTick, onWatcherCleanup } = require('vue')

const log = []
const a = ref(1)
const scope = effectScope()
scope.run(() => {
  watch(
    () => a.value > 0, // stays `true` when a goes 1 -> 2
    (value, _old, onCleanup) => {
      log.push(`cb(${value})`)
      onCleanup(() => log.push('onCleanup'))
      onWatcherCleanup(() => log.push('onWatcherCleanup'))
    },
    { immediate: true }, // same with flush: 'pre' | 'post' | 'sync'
  )
})

log.length = 0
a.value = 2
nextTick().then(() => {
  console.log('after a 1->2:', log)
  log.length = 0
  scope.stop()
  console.log('after stop():', log)
})
```

| version            | after `a` 1 → 2 (cb not called)      | after `scope.stop()`                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| 3.5.43             | `[]`                                 | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  |
| 3.6.0-alpha.1      | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  | `[]`                                 |
| 3.6.0-alpha.7      | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  | `[]`                                 |
| 3.6.0-beta.17      | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  | `[]`                                 |
| 3.6.0-rc.1         | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  | `[]`                                 |
| 3.6.0-rc.10        | `['onCleanup', 'onWatcherCleanup']`  | `[]`                                 |

Identical for `flush: 'pre'`, `'post'` and `'sync'`. A `computed` / ref / reactive source is not affected (the computed's dirty check stops the watcher from re-running).

### What is expected?

As in 3.5 and as documented: a cleanup registered with `onCleanup` or `onWatcherCleanup()` runs right before `cb` runs again, or when the watcher is stopped. Re-evaluating the getter to a value that did not change should leave the cleanups alone, so after `a` 1 → 2 nothing runs, and `scope.stop()` runs both cleanups.

### What is actually happening?

When a dependency of the getter changes, the watcher re-runs the getter and calls every cleanup `cb` registered **before** comparing values. The value is unchanged, so `cb` is not called and cannot register new cleanups. The watcher is now live but has none: whatever the cleanup tore down (a DOM listener, a timer, a subscription) is gone while the watcher keeps running, and `scope.stop()` later runs nothing.

### System Info

```shell
Node v24.21.0, macOS; reproduced in plain Node, no bundler.
```

### Any additional comments?

`ReactiveEffect.run()` (`packages/reactivity/src/effect.ts`) calls `cleanup(this)` unconditionally before running `fn`. `WatcherEffect` stores the callbacks of `onCleanup` / `onWatcherCleanup` (`boundCleanup` → `onWatcherCleanup(fn, false, this)`) in that same `cleanups` array, so `WatcherEffect.run()` → `super.run()` drains them while only re-evaluating the source. `WatcherEffect.run()` already calls `cleanup(this)` itself in the `hasChanged(...)` branch right before calling `cb` ("cleanup before running cb again"), which is the 3.5 behaviour; the unconditional call in the base `run()` makes it happen on every re-evaluation. In the 3.6.0-rc.10 build: `reactivity.cjs.js` around line 1448 (`ReactiveEffect.run`) and the `hasChanged` branch of `WatcherEffect.run` further down.

How we hit it: a composable takes a getter target (`() => (someOtherRef.value, el)`), attaches a `pointerdown` listener to the element in `cb` and removes it in `onCleanup`. Whenever the unrelated ref changes, the getter still returns the same element, the listener is removed and never re-attached, so the element silently stops responding. Nothing warns.

Possible fix direction (not tested): keep the base `cleanup(this)` for plain effects, but have `WatcherEffect` with a `cb` skip it (or keep `cb` cleanups apart from cleanups registered while the getter runs), so they only run in the `hasChanged` branch and on `stop()`.

pr.title: perf(build): remove preload link listeners on settle (fix #23920)
pr.body:
### What problem does this PR solve?

`__vitePreload()` attaches `load` / `error` listeners to the `<link rel="stylesheet">`
it generates for an async chunk's CSS, and never removes them. The link stays in
`document.head` for the page's lifetime, so those closures keep the whole preload
scope alive — including `baseModule`, the dynamic import factory passed by user code.

When that factory is defined inside a component or function scope, that scope is
retained as well. Repro (plain JS, no framework):
https://github.com/bpuns/vite-preload-listener-memory-leak

### Related issue

fixes #23920

### Alternatives considered

1. `{ once: true }` — insufficient: it only removes the listener that fired, so the
   other one stays attached and still retains the closure.
2. `build.modulePreload: false` — loses CSS preloading and only hides the symptom.
3. Chosen: one named handler bound to both events, removing both when either fires.

### What should reviewers focus on?

The behavior risk: `load` / `error` on a single stylesheet link fire at most once,
so removing both after settle cannot change observable behavior.

Tests:
- added a case in `playground/preload` asserting both listeners are removed
  (verified it fails without the fix: `expected 2 to be +0`)
- updated the `playground/js-sourcemap` inline snapshot, since the injected helper
  changed (same as #23662)

issue.title: Error with venv activation command for ksh on OpenBSD
issue.body:
On OpenBSD OS, `ksh` is the default shell (see https://man.openbsd.org/ksh).

With the latest version of `uv` (built from Git sources with Rust v1.98.1), creation of a virtual env. with `uv venv` command:
```sh
openbsd-dev$ echo $KSH_VERSION
@(#)PD KSH v5.2.14 99/07/13.2
openbsd-dev$ uv -V
uv 0.13.0 (x86_64-unknown-openbsd)

openbsd-dev$ uv venv
Using CPython 3.14.8 interpreter at: /usr/local/bin/python
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Activate with: source .venv/bin/activate
```

There is an **error when trying to activate venv** with the described command:
```sh
openbsd-dev$ source .venv/bin/activate
ksh: source: not found
```

Indeed, on OpenBSD with ksh shell, **`source` command does not exist**. To activate virtual env, the correct command is `. .venv/bin/activate`.

To fix this issue (output of venv activate command with ksh), I propose to modify this function (new case for `Shell::Ksh`) in `crates/uv/src/commands/venv.rs`:
https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/blob/a79aac95dc8f1d79e4396fdcb262d22c520cc1f6/crates/uv/src/commands/venv.rs#L389-L394

---

issue.title: [yaml] block scalar with trailing whitespace moves the next key to the root (main, after #19764)
issue.body:
**Prettier main (9d6c05b)**, not in 3.9.10

i couldn't use the playground for this since its on 3.9.10 and the bug is only on main. i ran it from a main checkout with `prettier.format(input, { parser: "yaml" })`.

```sh
# Options (if any):
--parser yaml
```

**Input:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

(there's a trailing space after `x`)

**Output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
c: 1
```

**Expected output:**

```yaml
a:
  b: |
    x 
  c: 1
```

**Why?**

`c: 1` gets moved out of `a` to the root, so the formatted file means something different. in a list it can even break the file, e.g. this github actions style input:

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
    name: x
  - name: second
```

comes out as

```yaml
steps:
  - run: |
      echo hi 
name: x
  - name: second
```

which doesn't parse anymore ("A block sequence may not be used as an implicit map key").

3.9.9 keeps the structure (it just strips the trailing space, which is what #19764 fixed). so i think this came in with #19764. looking at `src/language-yaml/print/block.js`, the last-line branch now emits a `literalline` when `hasTrailingContentWhitespace(node)` is true even if the block scalar isn't the last thing in its parent. that resets the indent for whatever gets printed next. probably it should only do that when the block scalar is the last node, or restore the indentation after it.

happy to send a PR with a test for the mapping and sequence cases if that helps.

pr.title: Fix YAML sibling indentation after block scalar with trailing whitespace
pr.body:
## Description

Fixes #20293.

#19764 preserves trailing whitespace in block scalars by ending the block with a `literalline`, so the doc printer doesn't trim it, and the mapping/sequence printer then omits its own `hardline`. A `literalline` goes back to the root indentation, so the next sibling was always printed at column 0 instead of the indentation of its mapping/sequence:

    a:           a:
      b: |         b: |
        x            x
      c: 1       c: 1      <- moved to the root

The item that ends with a block scalar with trailing whitespace now prints the line break itself, as `markAsRoot(literalline)`, right after its content and before `nextEmptyLine`. `literalline` keeps the whitespace from being trimmed, and `markAsRoot` makes it indent like `hardline`. The block only prints its own trailing line at the end of the file, and the root prints it between documents. Added format tests for nested mappings, a mapping in a sequence item (GitHub Actions style `- run: |` / `name:`), and nested sequences.

Thanks for fd, it comes in handy!

Finally `-1` overrides_with `--max-results`, but not the other way around so `fd --max-results=1 -1 -X prog query` will launch prog against all objects matching query.

### Describe what you expected to happen:

Consistent behavior: if mixing `max-results` with exec-type functions is refused, same should be true for aliases.

issue.title: Regression in 2.4.2: sdist install fails as root on Python < 3.10.12 / < 3.11.4 with TypeError: getgrnam() argument 'name' must be str, not None
issue.body:
### Description

Since 2.4.2, `poetry install` fails as root while extracting an sdist on Pythons whose `tarfile` has no `data_filter`. We hit it in a Docker build on `python:3.10.4-bullseye` with `crontab 1.0.4`, `facepy 1.0.12` and `PyMeeus 0.5.12`, which have no wheel on PyPI.

On these Pythons `extractall()` in `poetry/utils/helpers.py` uses the ported CPython 3.14 data filter added in #11027. The filter sets `uid`, `gid`, `uname` and `gname` to `None`, and members are then extracted with `archive.extract(member, dest, set_attrs=not member.isdir())`. As root, `tarfile._extract_member()` calls `chown()`, where these Python versions have no `None` guard:

```python
# CPython 3.10.11, tarfile.py
try:
    if grp:
        g = grp.getgrnam(tarinfo.gname)[2]
except KeyError:
    pass
```

`grp.getgrnam(None)` raises `TypeError`, which is not caught, and the install aborts. CPython has `if grp and tarinfo.gname:` there from 3.10.12 and 3.11.4 on.

Checked with the same command, `poetry install --no-root` of `crontab==1.0.4` as root:

| Python | poetry 2.4.2 | poetry 2.4.1 |
|---|---|---|
| 3.10.4 | fails | ok |
| 3.10.11 | fails | not checked |
| 3.10.12 | ok | not checked |
| 3.11.3 | fails | not checked |
| 3.11.4 | ok | not checked |
| 3.10.18 | ok | not checked |

In 2.4.1 the same fallback branch validated member paths only and did not change ownership attributes.

### Reproduction

```console
$ docker run --rm -u root python:3.10.4-bullseye bash -c '
  pip install -q "poetry==2.4.2"
  mkdir /t && cd /t
  printf "[project]\nname=\"repro\"\nversion=\"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python=\">=3.10\"\ndependencies=[\"crontab==1.0.4\"]\n" > pyproject.toml
  POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_CREATE=false poetry install --no-root'
```

The same command with `poetry==2.4.1` succeeds.

### Workarounds

- Run the install as a non-root user, verified on `python:3.10.4-bullseye` with 2.4.2.
- Use Python 3.10.12+ or 3.11.4+, verified above.
- Pin `poetry==2.4.1`.

**Poetry Installation Method:** pip

**Operating System:** Debian 11 (`python:3.10.4-bullseye` container), also seen on GitHub Actions `ubuntu-24.04`

**Poetry Version:** 2.4.2

installer.no-binary = null
installer.only-binary = null
installer.parallel = true
installer.re-resolve = false
solver.lazy-wheel = true

```

pr.title: Fix sdist extraction on older Python versions
pr.body:
## Summary

The tar security fallback clears ownership names with `None`. Python versions before 3.10.12 and 3.11.4 pass those values to `grp.getgrnam()` / `pwd.getpwnam()`, causing root sdist installs to fail.

Use empty ownership names instead, which preserves the ownership-stripping behavior without triggering the older tarfile bug. Added a regression test that simulates the affected tarfile implementation.

Fixes #11036.

issue.body:
**Version**
- `tokio v1.53.1`

**Platform**
`Linux $hostname 6.18.35 #1-NixOS SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Tue Jun  9 10:28:53 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux`

**Description**
[`Mutex`'s documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.53.1/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html) says:

> Tokio’s Mutex operates on a guaranteed FIFO basis. This means that the order in which tasks call the [`lock`](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.53.1/tokio/sync/struct.Mutex.html#method.lock) method is the exact order in which they will acquire the lock.

pr.title: sync: preserve FIFO lock order when coop budget is exhausted
pr.body:
Fixes #8365

### Problem
`Mutex` (and `Semaphore`) documentation states that lock acquisition operates on a guaranteed FIFO basis. However, in `Acquire::poll`, the cooperative-scheduling budget check `coop::poll_proceed(cx)` was performed *before* calling `semaphore.poll_acquire(...)`.

If a task's coop budget was exhausted before polling `lock().await`:
1. `coop::poll_proceed(cx)` returned `Poll::Pending`.
2. The future returned early without attempting `semaphore.poll_acquire(...)`.
3. The task's waiter node was never inserted into the semaphore's FIFO wait queue (`waiters.queue`).
4. If another task with remaining budget subsequently called `lock().await`, its waiter node was inserted into `waiters.queue` first.
5. When the lock was released, the second task acquired the lock before the first task, violating FIFO ordering.

### Solution
- Move `coop::poll_proceed(cx)` in `Acquire::poll` to run after `semaphore.poll_acquire(...)`. This ensures the waiter node is inserted into `waiters.queue` on its initial `poll()`, establishing its exact FIFO queue position.
- Update fast-path permit acquisition in `poll_acquire` to assign obtained permits to `node.state` via `node.assign_permits(...)`, ensuring state consistency if a coop budget yield occurs when returning ready.
- Update `needed` calculation in `poll_acquire` to load remaining permits directly from `node.state`.
- Add unit test `mutex_fifo_with_coop_budget` in `tests/sync_mutex.rs` verifying FIFO acquisition order when coop budget is depleted.

issue.title: Static file responses don't allow setting CORS headers (e.g., Access-Control-Allow-Origin)
issue.body:
Sinatra currently serves static files via the `static!` method, which bypasses all middleware and filters (e.g., `before`, `after`). This makes it impossible to add custom headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to responses for static assets in `public_folder`.

I've confirmed this behavior as follows:

- The `before` filter **does not run** when a static file is served. This is explicitly tested in the Sinatra test suite:  
  https://github.com/sinatra/sinatra/blob/cfcc70dee1133690207b5a3dc6000426ec04e250/test/filter_test.rb#L121

- The `send_file` method used internally by `static!` does not inject any custom headers beyond content-related defaults (e.g., content type, length). There's no hook to modify headers for static files.

- The [[sinatra-cross_origin](https://github.com/britg/sinatra-cross_origin)](https://github.com/britg/sinatra-cross_origin) gem does **not** apply to static files because it's based on middleware and route logic. Since static files are served before routes are hit, the gem has no opportunity to intervene.

This is a problem when serving images or fonts that need to be CORS-accessible (e.g., to be drawn onto a canvas). Without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, the browser blocks access to the data.

### Workarounds

I can serve static files through explicit routes like:

```ruby
get '/static/*' do |path|
  headers 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' => '*'
  send_file File.join(settings.public_folder, path)
end
```

…but this defeats the point of having a fast static file path, and loses benefits like automatic `static_cache_control`.

### Request

It would be helpful if Sinatra allowed either:

1. **A hook or setting** to inject headers into static file responses.
2. **Middleware support** for static file paths, or at least a way to apply `before`/`after` logic to static files optionally.
3. A **`static_headers` setting**, similar to `static_cache_control`, where one could define headers to be applied to all static responses.

Command-level regressions also reproduce the problem with legacy and mixed group declarations. With longer inclusion graphs, all-group removal can exhibit it when aggregate groups are declared before their included groups.

When using echo for a web application sending HTML and receiving MIMEApplicationForm POST requests, it seems very difficult / impossible to show helpful validation error messages to the user, when using `echo.context.bind()`. 

For any string data coming from the  MIMEApplicationForm submit which cannot be converted to the target type in the "DTO" struct provided, `echo.context.bind()`  returns a generic error that gives no information about which struct/form field failed validation. 

This makes it very difficult or impossible to render a helpful message to the user like "The `number` field should contain an integer". when the failed form is re-rendered in the browser. 

This issue is also discussed here:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/77712569/1087626

### Checklist

- [x] Dependencies installed
- [x] No typos
- [x] Searched existing issues and docs

For the error returned from `context.bind()` to return some information about which field failed type conversion

### Actual behaviour
The error returned from `context.bind()` contains no information about the form field which failed type conversion.

```bash
server as below, then POST a non-integer to be bound into an integer field

$ curl localhost:8080/submit -d"number=10a"
code=400, message=strconv.ParseInt: parsing "10a": invalid syntax, internal=strconv.ParseInt: parsing "10a": invalid syntax

```go

		}
		return c.String(http.StatusOK, fmt.Sprint(dto) + "\n")

pr.title: fix: use the first valid fallback role in `role` for a11y checks
pr.body:
The `role` attribute can list fallback roles, such as `role="switch checkbox"`. The checks that run per token, like `a11y_unknown_role`, already split the value. The element-level checks that run after them still used the whole string as the role. Because the full string matched no known role, an element with fallback roles was treated as if it had no role, and that caused false positives:

- `a11y_no_noninteractive_tabindex` and `a11y_no_static_element_interactions` on `<div role="switch checkbox" tabindex="0" ...>`
- `a11y_click_events_have_key_events` and `a11y_no_static_element_interactions` on `<div role="none presentation" onclick={...}>`
- `a11y_role_supports_aria_props` was skipped, so unsupported ARIA attributes went unreported

This change resolves the static `role` value to the first token that is a known, non-abstract role, as browsers do. If no token is valid, it falls back to the first token, so unknown roles behave as before. Surrounding whitespace no longer affects the result either.

The new `a11y-fallback-roles` validator sample fails without the change (10 incorrect warnings, and the expected `a11y_role_supports_aria_props` warning is missing) and passes with it.

issue.title: compileSerializationSchema passes null for omitted optional metadata
issue.body:
### Description

Calling `reply.compileSerializationSchema(schema)` without optional metadata passes `null` for both `httpStatus` and `contentType` to a custom serializer compiler. The public types model those fields as optional strings, and the documentation describes the default as `undefined`.

This is present on `main` at `1beaf7e72d24b2fc63a02a7f5806772a00e45454`:

- [The implementation defaults both parameters to `null`](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/1beaf7e72d24b2fc63a02a7f5806772a00e45454/lib/reply.js#L373-L397)
- [`FastifyRouteSchemaDef` declares optional string fields](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/1beaf7e72d24b2fc63a02a7f5806772a00e45454/types/schema.d.ts#L18-L25)
- [The reference says the optional status defaults to `undefined`](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/1beaf7e72d24b2fc63a02a7f5806772a00e45454/docs/Reference/Reply.md#L78-L86)

### Reproduction

```js
const Fastify = require('fastify')

const app = Fastify()

app.setSerializerCompiler((definition) => {
  console.log(definition.httpStatus, definition.contentType)
  return JSON.stringify
})

app.get('/', (_request, reply) => {
  const serialize = reply.compileSerializationSchema({ type: 'object' })
  return serialize({ ok: true })
})

app.inject({ method: 'GET', url: '/' })
```

### Actual behavior

The custom compiler receives `null, null`.

### Expected behavior

It should receive `undefined, undefined`, consistent with the optional TypeScript fields and documented default, or the public type/documentation should explicitly include `null`.

### Possible direction

Default the implementation parameters to `undefined` (or omit the properties when they were not supplied). This would preserve the existing optional contract for custom compilers.

I found this while benchmarking an automated code-review workflow and manually verified the source path and reproduction before reporting it.

pr.title: fix: omit absent compileSerializationSchema metadata instead of passing null
pr.body:
Closes #6988.

`compileSerializationSchema` defaulted both optional parameters to `null`:

```js
function (schema, httpStatus = null, contentType = null)
```

so a custom serializer compiler called through `reply.compileSerializationSchema(schema)` received `null` for both. `FastifyRouteSchemaDef` declares them as optional strings and the reference docs describe the default as `undefined`, so the implementation was the odd one out. `serializeInput` already declares the same two parameters without defaults and forwards `undefined`, so this also makes the two paths agree.

Dropping the defaults is the whole change. Existing tests that touch this assert `!httpStatus` rather than a specific value, so they hold either way, and I could not find anywhere in `lib`, `test` or `types` that compares this to `null`.

Added one test asserting both values arrive as `undefined` when the metadata is not supplied. It fails without the change.

Verified locally: `node --test test/internals/*.test.js` gives 395 passed / 0 failed, `npm run test:types` passes all 16 files and 1282 assertions, and eslint is clean on both touched files.

I left a separate note on #6987 about the cache-keying half, since fixing that one has a public API consequence for `getSerializationFunction` and I would rather agree the approach first.

pr.title: fix(python): preserve variant in `uv python upgrade`
pr.body:
## Summary

Fixes #22831.

Previously, running `uv python upgrade` without explicit version targets failed to upgrade free-threaded (or other non-default variant) managed Python installations:

1. `From<&ManagedPythonInstallation> for PythonDownloadRequest` hardcoded `PythonVariant::Default` instead of preserving `key.variant` when constructing the download request for installed managed Pythons. As a result, `uv python upgrade` and `uv python install --reinstall` converted free-threaded installations (e.g., `3.14t`) into default-variant requests (`3.14`).
2. `requested_minor_versions` in `crates/uv-python-commands/src/install.rs` tracked only `(major, minor)` tuples from `PythonRequest::Version(VersionRequest::MajorMinor(..))`, ignoring both the `PythonVariant` and `PythonRequest::Key(download_request)` entries created by bare `uv python upgrade`.

This change:
- Preserves `key.variant` in `From<&ManagedPythonInstallation> for PythonDownloadRequest`.
- Tracks `(major, minor, variant)` in `requested_minor_versions` across both `PythonRequest::Version` and `PythonRequest::Key` so `upgradeable` filtering matches the exact variant being upgraded.

## Test Plan

- Added unit test `test_download_request_from_installation_preserves_variant` in `crates/uv-python-managed/src/managed.rs`.
- Extended `python_upgrade_without_version` in `crates/uv/tests/python/python_upgrade.rs` to verify bare `uv python upgrade` upgrades an installed `3.13.1t` to the latest `3.13t` patch release alongside standard installations.

issue.title: Include the HTTP QUERY method in RouterGroup.Any
issue.body:
### Feature Description

## Feature description

`RouterGroup.Any` currently registers a fixed list of HTTP methods but excludes `QUERY`, even though Gin supports `router.QUERY` and `gin.MethodQuery` (RFC 10008). As a result, a `QUERY` request to an `Any` route returns 404.

```go
r := gin.New()
r.Any("/search", func(c *gin.Context) {
    c.Status(http.StatusOK)
})
// QUERY /search currently returns 404.
```

I propose adding `gin.MethodQuery` to the methods registered by `Any`, then updating its documentation and routing tests. This would make `Any` cover every HTTP method that Gin exposes through a routing shortcut. Applications that want an explicit set of methods can continue using `Match`.

## Compatibility consideration

PR #4806 deliberately left `QUERY` out of `Any` to preserve the matching behavior of existing routes. Including it would change those routes to accept `QUERY`, so this should be treated as an intentional behavior change and called out in release notes. Handlers registered with `Any` would also need to respect QUERY's safe and idempotent semantics when processing that method.

Related: #4721 and #4806.

issue.title: Request.url turns a // path into an authority when the scope has no host
issue.body:
When a request scope has neither a `Host` header nor a `server` entry, `Request.url` places `scope["path"]` directly after the scheme, so a path that starts with `//` is parsed as an authority. A response built from that URL then emits a scheme-relative `Location`.

### Reproduction

```python
from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import RedirectResponse

scope = {
    "type": "http",
    "scheme": "http",
    "path": "//evil.example/x",
    "query_string": b"a=1",
    "headers": [],
    "server": None,
}

url = Request(scope).url
print(str(url), url.netloc)
print(RedirectResponse(url).headers["location"])
```

On current `main` (1.7.0) this prints:

```text
//evil.example/x?a=1 evil.example
//evil.example/x?a=1
```

The `Location` value is scheme-relative, so a browser resolves it to `http://evil.example/x?a=1`.

As soon as any origin information is present the result is same-origin, which is the expected behaviour:

```python
scope["headers"] = [(b"host", b"victim.example")]   # or scope["server"] = ("victim.example", 80)
# -> http://victim.example//evil.example/x?a=1
```

### Why this looks wrong

#3326 says the path should not be placed directly against the authority and that the resulting URL should parse back into the components it was built from. That holds when `Host` or `server` is available, but the branch that builds the URL without origin metadata still uses the raw path as the whole URL, so the path ends up in `netloc`.

`server` is optional in the ASGI HTTP scope, so a scope without it and without a `Host` header is legal. An application that redirects to `request.url` then sends the visitor to the host taken from the path.

### Suggested fix

In the branch that builds the URL without origin metadata, keep a `//`-prefixed path out of the authority position, for example by percent-encoding its first character or by producing a URL without a netloc, so `urlsplit` cannot turn the first path segment into a host.

pr.title: Escape path delimiters and leading `//` when building URLs
pr.body:
`scope["path"]` is percent-decoded, but `URL` placed it into the URL string as is, so some path characters changed how the URL was parsed:

- `?` and `#` started the query string or the fragment.
- `\` is not a valid URL character.
- A leading `//` was parsed as the authority when the scope had no `Host` header or `server`.

`url_path_for` had the same `//` case, for example `Route("/{path:path}")` with `path="/foo"`.

This percent-encodes `?`, `#` and `\` in the scope path, encodes `\` in `url_path_for`, and escapes a leading `//` as `/%2F`, the same as Django's `escape_leading_slashes`.

Closes #3579. Supersedes [#3586](https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/pull/3586), thanks @SulimanAbdulrazzaq for the `?`/`#` part.

This PR was developed with the assistance of either Claude or Codex. I've reviewed and verified the changes.

pr.title: Start @StartStop MockWebServer for @Nested JUnit 5 tests
pr.body:
Fixes #9546.

A `@StartStop MockWebServer` field declared on an outer class is never started when the test runs inside a `@Nested` inner class, so a nested test that uses the server fails with `IllegalStateException: call start() first`.

`StartStopExtension.beforeEach` resolved instance fields from `context.testInstance` (the innermost `@Nested` instance) and `context.requiredTestClass` (the nested class). The fix walks `context.requiredTestInstances.allInstances`, which returns every instance in the enclosing hierarchy, and starts the annotated fields on each. Behavior is unchanged for non-nested tests, where `allInstances` is the single test instance.

Fixes #830: a handler sharing a pattern with a `Route()`/`Mount()` call was invisible to `Walk()`/`Routes()`, because the mount's internal stub handler caused the whole node to be hidden.

```go
r.Route("/foo", func(r chi.Router) {
    r.Route("/bar", func(r chi.Router) { r.Get("/{id}", h) })

})

- Drops #1146's unrelated `walk()` change (`continue`/`subrouteMw`) — reverting just that half still passes everything.

pr.title: fix(interceptors): tolerate nullish handlers in syncHandlerEntries
pr.body:
:surfer:

Fixes #11114

## Problem

`syncHandlerEntries()` reads `handlers.length` before checking that `handlers` exists, so assigning a falsy value to the public `handlers` array makes every subsequent request throw:

```js
axios.interceptors.request.use(config => config);
axios.interceptors.request.handlers = null;
await axios.get('https://example.com');
// TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'length')
```

`clear()` has always guarded with `if (this.handlers)`, and `utils.forEach` returns early on nullish input, so a falsy `handlers` array was a tolerated state on v1.19.0. This is a regression from #11087 (merged, unreleased).

## Fix

Three reads were unguarded, not one:

- `syncHandlerEntries` — the `else if (handlers.length !== ...)` branch **and** the trailing `internals.handlersLength = handlers.length`. Both now use a `countHandlers()` helper that treats nullish as an empty stack.
- `trimHandlers` — returns early instead of dereferencing.
- the `forEach` `finally` block — `internals.handlersLength = this.handlers.length` had the same problem and now goes through the same helper.

Fixing only `syncHandlerEntries` leaves the `finally` block throwing on the way out of the first `forEach`, so both paths are covered.

## Tests

8 cases, parametrized over `null` and `undefined`:

- `forEach` is a no-op rather than throwing
- a **repeated** `forEach` stays safe — this takes the `handlers === handlersRef` branch, which is where the stack trace in the report actually lands, and it isn't reached by a single call
- `eject` does not throw
- the manager recovers once `handlers` is restored to an array

All 8 fail on `v1.x` with the reported `TypeError` and pass with this change.

## Verification

`npx vitest run --project unit`: **1001 passed, 1 failed**. The single failure is `tests/unit/adapters/fetch.test.js > should not use inherited Symbol.iterator for request headers`, which fails identically on a clean checkout — unrelated to this change. `npx eslint lib/core/InterceptorManager.js` is clean.

## Not included

The report mentions two further items from the same change, deliberately left out to keep this focused on the crash — happy to follow up on either:

- `eject(String(id))` silently no-ops now that lookups go through a `Map` rather than an array index.
- `tests/unit/core/InterceptorManager.test.js:32` indexes handlers by id, which only holds while nothing below those slots is trimmed.

No `PRE_RELEASE_CHANGELOG.md` entry: per `AGENTS.md` that file tracks user-visible unreleased changes, and this crash never shipped — v1.19.0 behaves correctly. Happy to add one if you'd prefer it recorded.


---
## Summary by cubic
Prevents a TypeError when interceptor handlers are set to null or undefined by treating them as empty and restoring them on `use()`. Previously `syncHandlerEntries` and the `forEach` cleanup read `.length` unguarded and could crash; now both paths are safe and behavior matches prior tolerant releases.

**Details**

issue.title: dump() of a long double value is corrupt under a locale with a multibyte decimal point (glibc ps_AF)

pr.title: Replace a multibyte decimal point in dump() of a long double
pr.body:
Fixes #5993.

## What

`dump_float(number_float_t, std::false_type)`, the `snprintf` path for a `number_float_t` that is neither IEEE single nor double (a `long double` on x86-64 and aarch64 Linux), read `localeconv()->decimal_point` and `->thousands_sep` as single `char`s. Under a locale whose decimal point is a multibyte sequence (glibc's `ps_AF`: U+066B, bytes `D9 AB`; thousands separator U+066C, `D9 AC`), it removed the shared first byte `D9` as a "thousands separator" and left `AB` in the output: `1.5L` dumped as `1\xab5.0`, which does not parse back.

Now the decimal point is treated as a byte string, as `convert_float_locale_aware()` already does on the parse side (#5660): `std::search` finds the whole sequence, which is replaced by `.`, and the rest of the buffer moves left. The thousands-separator removal is gone: `%g` never groups digits (that needs the POSIX `'` flag), so it had nothing legitimate to remove.

Default `json` (double) and `float` are not affected; they use `to_chars`.

## Tests

`unit-locale-cpp.cpp`, "locale with a multi-byte decimal point": under each available multibyte locale, `dump()` of `1.5L`, `2.0L`, `-0.25L` gives the C-locale text, and `1.5e-7L` and the parsed long double array round-trip through `dump()`/`parse()`.

Run in `gcc:16` (glibc 2.41) with generated `ps_AF.UTF-8`, `fa_IR.UTF-8`, `de_DE.UTF-8`: the new checks fail without the fix (`1\xab5.0`, parse_error.101) and pass with it; `unit-locale-cpp` and `unit-serialization` pass in full. (CI runners may not have `ps_AF`; the test then skips with a message, as before.)

## Public API

No breaking changes. `dump()` output changes only where it was corrupt (a non-binary64 `long double` under a locale with a multibyte decimal point).

issue.title: approx with timedelta: rel parameter treated as absolute tolerance despite its name
issue.body:
Was playing around with the new `approx` datetime/timedelta support and noticed something weird about how `rel` works for timedelta.

For numbers, `rel` is a relative tolerance -- a fraction of the expected value:

    approx(100, rel=0.05)  # within 5% of 100

But for timedelta, `rel` just acts as another absolute tolerance. It gets merged with `abs` via `max()`:

    approx(timedelta(seconds=100), rel=timedelta(seconds=5), abs=timedelta(seconds=2))
    # tolerance = max(5s, 2s) = 5s -- not 5% of anything

The confusing part is that the parameter is called `rel` and the TypeError message says "relative tolerance for timedelta must be a timedelta", but the behavior is purely absolute. The relevant code in `ApproxTimedelta.__init__` (around line 594):

    tolerance = max(t for t in (abs, rel) if t is not None)

So `rel` and `abs` are effectively the same thing for timedelta -- whichever is larger wins. I get that multiplying two timedeltas does not work, but then maybe `rel` should just be rejected for timedelta the same way it is for datetime? Or accept a float and compute `rel * expected` (timedelta * float does work).

Not sure what the right fix is, just found this surprising when I tried using `rel` and realized it was not doing what I expected.

pr.title: fix approx rel for timedelta: accept float, compute rel * expected
pr.body:
Was looking into #14462 and noticed that the `rel` param for timedelta in `approx` was being treated as an absolute tolerance -- merged with `abs` via `max()` instead of being scaled by the expected value. So `approx(timedelta(seconds=100), rel=timedelta(seconds=5))` gave you a flat 5-second tolerance, not 5% of 100 seconds.

The fix makes `rel` accept a float for timedelta comparisons, same as it works for numbers. Now `approx(td, rel=0.05)` means "within 5% of the expected timedelta", which is what you'd naturally expect from a parameter called `rel`. The tolerance is computed as `rel * abs(expected)`, which works because `timedelta * float` returns a timedelta in Python.

When both `rel` and `abs` are provided, the larger tolerance wins (same as `ApproxScalar`).

`rel` for datetime is still rejected with the same TypeError as before.

Closes #14462

issue.title: `post_message` is thread-unsafe now that `_message_queue` is a `cached_property`
issue.body:
## The bug

Memray's test suite hangs under Python 3.8 when run with Textual 3.3.0, and bisecting points to bc96aac149aadd5778a0bf65a9be6df609a60f4b as the commit that breaks us. If I ctrl-c the hanging test suite I see:
```text
pytest.PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning: Exception in thread Thread-1

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/godlygeek/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.8.20-linux-x86_64-gnu/lib/python3.8/threading.py", line 932, in _bootstrap_inner
    self.run()
  File "/home/godlygeek/repos/memray/.38/lib/python3.8/site-packages/memray/reporters/tui.py", line 734, in run
    self._app.post_message(
  File "/home/godlygeek/3ps/textual/src/textual/message_pump.py", line 841, in post_message
    loop.call_soon_threadsafe(self._message_queue.put_nowait, message)
  File "/home/godlygeek/3ps/textual/src/textual/_compat.py", line 57, in __get__
    val = self.func(instance)
  File "/home/godlygeek/3ps/textual/src/textual/message_pump.py", line 150, in _message_queue
    return asyncio.Queue()
  File "/home/godlygeek/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.8.20-linux-x86_64-gnu/lib/python3.8/asyncio/queues.py", line 35, in __init__
    self._loop = events.get_event_loop()
  File "/home/godlygeek/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.8.20-linux-x86_64-gnu/lib/python3.8/asyncio/events.py", line 639, in get_event_loop
    raise RuntimeError('There is no current event loop in thread %r.'
RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'Thread-1'.
```

This seems to be a genuine regression in Textual. After Textual 3.3.0, there's a race condition in Textual apps where things fail if the first access to an app's message pump happens from a different thread than the app is running in. Our test suite deterministically provokes that race condition by calling `app.post_message` from a background thread while the app is still being mounted.

Now that `_message_queue` is a cached property, it's possible that the first access to it (and thus the queue's lazy creation) happens not from the thread that the app is running in but from a different thread (which is allowed to happen because `post_message` is documented to be thread safe). If that happens, the created `asyncio.Queue` will associate itself with the event loop for the thread that `post_message` is being called from, instead of the thread that the app is running in.

pr.title: sync primitives
pr.body:
Fixes https://github.com/Textualize/textual/issues/5845

A recent update made the threading objects instantiate lazily, with cached_property. This was done because in Python3.8 objects like Event are bound to the thread where they are instantiated, and would break if you tried to use them in another thread with a different async loop.

Unfortunately that fix broke the thread safety of post_message. This update forces the async primitives to instantiate in the async task where they are used.

This is a bit of a patch until we drop 3.8 (soon).

issue.title: Excessive memory retention in v4 memoizer
issue.body:
We are seeing a severe memory regression after upgrading Zod from 4.4.3 to 4.5.4 in a large Backstage monorepo.

The workload is a repository-wide ESLint run:

```sh
yarn eslint . --no-cache
```

With Zod 4.4.3 it completes normally:

```text
Elapsed time: 49.16s
Maximum RSS: 5,487,520 KB
Exit status: 0
```

With Zod 4.5.4, even with an 8 GiB limit, it eventually runs out of memory:

```text
Elapsed time before OOM: 181.32s
Maximum RSS before OOM: 8,723,528 KB
Exit status: 1
```

The final GC cycles look like this:

```text
Mark-Compact 8042.9 (8224.5) -> 8027.5 (8225.2) MB
Mark-Compact 8043.5 (8225.2) -> 8028.1 (8225.7) MB

FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit
Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

I traced the regression to the `lastCtx` / `lastBucket` cache in `src/v4/core/memoizer.ts`.

Current code:

```ts
let lastCtx: object | undefined;
let lastBucket: Map<object, Entry> | undefined;

// ...

let bucket: Map<object, Entry>;

if (lastCtx === ctx) {
  bucket = lastBucket!;
} else {
  bucket = bucketFor(state, inst);
  lastCtx = ctx;
  lastBucket = bucket;
}
```

Removing this additional cache and always retrieving the bucket from the parse state fixes the problem:

```ts
const bucket = bucketFor(state, inst);
```

With that change applied to Zod 4.5.4:

```text
Elapsed time: 48.44s
Maximum RSS: 5,621,244 KB
Exit status: 0
```

Here are teh results:

| Version | Result | Time | Maximum RSS |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4.4.3 | success | 49.16s | 5,487,520 KB |
| 4.5.4 | OOM | 181.32s | 8,723,528 KB |
| 4.5.4 with cache removed | success | 48.44s | 5,621,244 KB |

The comment above the cache says that the bucket is memoized "for one parse", but `lastCtx` and `lastBucket` are captured by the closure created in `attach(inst)`. This means the most recent context and bucket can remain reachable for the lifetime of the schema instance.

The per-parse state already keeps the bucket, so the extra `lastCtx` / `lastBucket` fast path appears to extend the lifetime of parse-local data unnecessarily.

Is there a reason this cache needs to live on the schema instance rather than relying on `bucketFor(state, inst)`?

pr.title: fix(v4): stop the memoizer from pinning a finished parse
pr.body:
Fixes #6557.

A recursive schema held the entire input and output graph of its last parse until the next parse replaced it. The memoizer caches the current parse context and its bucket on the schema instance, so a re-entered container skips a lookup — but nothing ever clears that slot, and it outlives the parse. One long-lived schema therefore pinned every object the parse touched, across every schema in it. Reported as an 8 GiB OOM on a repo-wide ESLint run that completed on 4.4.3.

The buckets only ever need `get` and `set`, and the back-edge set only needs `add` and `has`. Making the parse state weak throughout leaves the fast path exactly as it is and lets the graph go.

### Measurements

| axis | main | this PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| retained after one parse | 10.1 MB | 2.2 MB |
| recursive parse, object + array | 5694/s | 5354/s (−6.0%) |
| recursive parse, self-referential object | 10607/s | 9873/s (−6.9%) |
| bundle, classic | 21560 B gz | 21564 B gz |
| bundle, mini | 3710 B gz | 3710 B gz |

Retention is a `WeakRef` probe plus a heap measurement over one parse of a 29k-node tree, with the input dropped and GC forced. The 2.2 MB residual is `WeakMap` table capacity rather than live data — the input collects, and the next parse of the same schema replaces the tables.

Throughput is medians of 8 interleaved rounds, fixed iteration count with `gc()` between samples. The cost lands only on schemas that can re-enter themselves; the memoizer takes its own wrapper back off every other schema on first parse. Load average was 9–13 during the runs, so treat the magnitudes as approximate — the ordering held across every round.

The regression test asserts the parsed input is collectable. It reaches the collector through `v8.setFlagsFromString`, the way the existing release-the-parsed-input test in `error.test.ts` already does, so no test config changes.

### Alternatives

Deleting the fast path, as the issue proposes, removes the retention completely but measured 13–17% slower on the same two shapes. Scoping it to the parse state, proposed later in the thread, recovers the speed only when a single container re-enters itself; on an object holding an array of itself the slot thrashes and it is no better than deleting the cache.

Reported by @alexvoedi, with alternative benchmarks from @0jaspahwa in the thread.

issue.title: Per-domain / per-slot concurrency is not enforced with the asyncio reactor when download delay is 0
issue.body:
## Description

With the asyncio reactor and no download delay, a download slot's concurrency limit is
not enforced.

In the reproduction below, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2` lets 18
requests to one host run at once; the server confirms it receives all 18 together. A
`DOWNLOAD_SLOTS` entry with `concurrency` and no `delay` behaves the same way, as it
goes through the same code.

Scrapy's own defaults hit this case (asyncio reactor, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 8`,
`DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 0`). With them, the same script reaches up to 15 simultaneous requests
to one host against the limit of 8. The exact peak varies between runs, and
`CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 16` caps how far it can go. Projects generated by `startproject` set
`DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 1`, which hides it.

## Steps to reproduce

Self-contained, no network access needed: it serves its own endpoint on localhost.

```python
"""Minimal reproduction: per-slot concurrency is not enforced when delay is 0.

Serves a local endpoint that holds each response open for HOLD seconds, sends
BURST requests to it with CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2 and no download
delay, and reports the largest number of requests in flight at any one time,
both as Scrapy counts them (the slot) and as the server sees them.

    $ python mre.py                    # asyncio reactor -> peak 18, limit ignored
    $ DELAY=0.05 python mre.py         # non-zero delay  -> peak 2
    $ REACTOR=select python mre.py     # SelectReactor   -> peak 2
"""
import os
import threading
import time
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

import scrapy
from scrapy.crawler import CrawlerProcess
from twisted.internet.task import LoopingCall

CONCURRENCY = 2
BURST = 20
HOLD = 0.25                                # how long each response is held open
DELAY = float(os.environ.get("DELAY", 0))  # DOWNLOAD_DELAY
REACTOR = {
    "asyncio": "twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor",
    "select": "twisted.internet.selectreactor.SelectReactor",
}[os.environ.get("REACTOR", "asyncio")]


_lock = threading.Lock()
_in_flight = 0
_server_peak = 0


class _Endpoint(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"

    def do_GET(self):
        global _in_flight, _server_peak
        with _lock:
            _in_flight += 1
            _server_peak = max(_server_peak, _in_flight)
        time.sleep(HOLD)
        with _lock:
            _in_flight -= 1
        body = b"ok"
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass


_server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), _Endpoint)
PORT = _server.server_address[1]
threading.Thread(target=_server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()


class BurstSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "burst"
    custom_settings = {
        # Far above the per-domain limit, so the slot is the only thing that
        # could bound this traffic.
        "CONCURRENT_REQUESTS": 100,
        "CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN": CONCURRENCY,
        "DOWNLOAD_DELAY": DELAY,
        "LOG_LEVEL": "ERROR",
        "TWISTED_REACTOR": REACTOR,
    }

    peak = 0
    started = None

    async def start(self):
        self.started = time.monotonic()
        self._sampler = LoopingCall(self._sample)
        self._sampler.start(0.001)
        for i in range(BURST):
            yield scrapy.Request(f"http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/{i}", dont_filter=True)

    def parse(self, response):
        return

    def _sample(self):
        slot = self.crawler.engine.downloader.slots.get("127.0.0.1")
        if slot is not None:
            self.peak = max(self.peak, len(slot.transferring))

    def closed(self, reason):
        self._sampler.stop()
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - self.started
        print(f"\n  reactor                     : {REACTOR.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}")
        print(f"  download delay              : {DELAY}")
        print(f"  concurrency per domain      : {CONCURRENCY}")
        print(f"  requests sent               : {BURST}")
        print(f"  peak len(slot.transferring) : {self.peak}")
        print(f"  peak requests at the server : {_server_peak}")
        print(f"  elapsed                     : {elapsed:.2f}s "
              f"(at {CONCURRENCY} at a time: ~{BURST / CONCURRENCY * HOLD:.2f}s)\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    process = CrawlerProcess(settings={"TELNETCONSOLE_ENABLED": False})
    process.crawl(BurstSpider)
    process.start()
```

## Expected behaviour

No more than 2 requests in flight to the host at once, so 20 requests at 0.25 s each
take roughly 2.5 s.

## Actual behaviour

```
  reactor                     : AsyncioSelectorReactor
  download delay              : 0.0
  concurrency per domain      : 2
  requests sent               : 20
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 18          <- expected <= 2
  peak requests at the server : 18          <- expected <= 2
  elapsed                     : 0.54s       <- expected ~2.50s
```

Either a non-zero delay or a non-asyncio reactor gives the expected result, which is
what points at the cause:

```
$ DELAY=0.05 python mre.py
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 2
  peak requests at the server : 2
  elapsed                     : 2.63s

$ REACTOR=select python mre.py
  peak len(slot.transferring) : 2
  peak requests at the server : 2
  elapsed                     : 2.56s
```

The peak is 18 on almost every run, occasionally 19, depending on how many requests the
engine has fed before the first transfer registers.

## Diagnosis

`Downloader._process_queue`:

```python
while slot.queue and slot.free_transfer_slots() > 0:
    slot.lastseen = now
    request, queue_dfd = slot.queue.popleft()
    download_dfd = deferred_from_coro(
        self._wait_for_download(slot, request, queue_dfd)
    )
    ...
    # prevent burst if inter-request delays were configured
    if delay:
        self._process_queue(slot)
        break
```

`free_transfer_slots()` is `concurrency - len(slot.transferring)`, but
`slot.transferring.add(request)` happens inside `_download`. Under the asyncio reactor,
`deferred_from_coro` wraps the coroutine in an asyncio task, which doesn't start until
the loop yields. So `len(slot.transferring)` can't grow while this loop runs,
`free_transfer_slots()` returns the same value on every iteration, and the loop drains
the whole queue.

Two things hide it:

- **A delay.** The `if delay:` branch stops after one request and re-arms through
  `latercall`, so the count is up to date by the time the loop runs again.
- **A non-asyncio reactor.** There the coroutine runs straight away, up to its first
  real suspension, which is past the `transferring.add`, so the count is already current.

(In 2.18.0 the line is `_schedule_coro(...)`, which calls `loop.create_task` under
asyncio; same effect.)

## Possible fix

Counting a request as transferring when it is popped, rather than when its coroutine
starts, keeps `free_transfer_slots()` accurate inside the loop:

```diff
 request, queue_dfd = slot.queue.popleft()
+slot.transferring.add(request)
 download_dfd = deferred_from_coro(
```

`_download` already adds the request to the same set (a second add does nothing) and
removes it in its `finally`. 

When applying this in a fork, this gives:

| | slot peak | server peak | elapsed | responses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| master, `delay 0` | 18 | 18 | 0.53 s | 20/20 |
| patched, `delay 0` | **2** | **2** | 2.56 s | 20/20 |
| patched, `delay 0.05` | 2 | 2 | 2.64 s | 20/20 |
| patched, Scrapy defaults (limit 8) | 8 | 8 | 1.28 s | 40/40 |


## Versions

```
Scrapy       : 2.19.0
Python       : 3.12.14
Twisted      : 26.4.0
lxml         : 6.1.3
Platform     : macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Reactor      : twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor
```

The `pulumi` module renders an empty `$stack` on Pulumi v3.256.0 and later.

#### Expected Behavior

`$stack` shows the selected stack, as it does on Pulumi v3.255.0 and earlier.

#### Additional context/Screenshots

pulumi/pulumi#23974 ("fix(cli): scope current stack selection to the active backend", first released in v3.256.0) changed the workspace settings file so that the selected stack is scoped to the backend it belongs to:

```jsonc
// ~/.pulumi/workspaces/<project>-<sha1>-workspace.json, before

}

// after

    .get("stack")?
    .as_str()

Read `stacks[<backend url>]`, resolving the active backend the way the CLI does (`PULUMI_BACKEND_URL`, then the project's `backend.url`, then `current` in `credentials.json`), and keep the old `stack` key as a fallback for workspace files that have not been rewritten yet. Happy to open a PR.

## Description

Fixes #7723

Pulumi v3.256.0 ([pulumi/pulumi#23974](https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/pull/23974)) scoped the selected stack to the active backend, changing the workspace settings file:

```jsonc
// ~/.pulumi/workspaces/<project>-<sha1>-workspace.json, before

    "stack": "acme/infra/dev"
}

// after
{
    "stacks": {
        "https://api.pulumi.com": "acme/infra/dev"
    }
}
```

Pulumi still reads the old `stack` key, but no longer writes it, so `$stack` silently goes empty after the first `pulumi stack select` on a new enough CLI.

This reads the new map, picking the entry for the backend in use. The backend is resolved the same way the CLI resolves it in `GetCurrentCloudURLWithSource`:

1. `PULUMI_BACKEND_URL`
2. the project's `backend.url` in `Pulumi.yaml`
3. `current` in `credentials.json` (already parsed by this module for `$username`)

pr.title: walk: Flush stdout in batches
pr.body:
The previous behaviour was designed to mimic the output buffering of
typical UNIX tools: line-buffered if stdout is a TTY, and fully-buffered
otherwise.  More precicely, when printing to a terminal, fd would flush
explicitly after printing any buffered results, then flush after every
single result once streaming mode started.  When not printing to a
terminal, fd never explicitly flushed, so writes would only happen as
the BufWriter filled up.

The new behaviour actually unifies the TTY and non-TTY cases: we flush
after printing the buffered results, then once we start streaming, we
flush after each batch, but *only when the channel is empty*.  This
provides a good balance: if the channel is empty, the receiver thread
might as well flush before it goes to sleep waiting for more results.
If the channel is non-empty, we might as well process those results
before deciding to flush.

For TTYs, this should improve performance by consolidating write() calls
without sacrificing interactivity.  For non-TTYs, we'll be flushing more
often, but only when the receiver would otherwise have nothing to do,
thus improving interactivity without sacrificing performance.  This is
particularly handy when fd is piped into another command (such as head
or grep): with the old behaviour, fd could wait for the whole traversal
to finish before printing anything.  With the new behaviour, fd will
print those results soon after they are received.

Fixes #1313.
